description:
Black Willow (Salix nigra)

7 July 2016
Unicorn Lake 
Denton, Denton County, Texas

Unicorn Lake is a man-made lake that's only a few years old and therefore the Black Willow trees presented in this observation reflect their still relatively young age and smaller size. Black Willow is a native hardwood tree of North America. Black Willow grows best near bodies of water and requires substantial amounts of water to grow and thrive. It grows from the eastern half of Canada south to the Florida Panhandle thence west to Texas, Oklahoma and southeastern Colorado providing the farthest western extension in the continental United States. But it also extends south into Mexico and grows all along the Río Bravo/Río Grande hence it is found in at least Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, and perhaps extends beyond these northeastern states as well. Additional common names for Black Willow are many and include Gulf Black Willow, Swamp Willow, and Mexicans came to call it Sauz, Spanish for willow. There’s a small rural community in South Texas in Starr County called El Sauz, Texas (aka Willow, Texas). Still other common names for Black Willow in French and English include: American Willow, Brittle Willow, Champlain Willow, Dudley Willow, Gooding Willow, Puzzle Willow, Rough American Willow, Scythe-leaf Willow, Scythe-leaved Willow, Southwestern Black Willow, Tall Black Willow, Texas Black Willow, Western Black Willow, as well as Sauce, Saule, Saule Noir, Swamp Walnut, Weide, Wilg, Willow, and Willow Catkins. Black Willow is a member of the Willow family of trees (Salicaceae) and is considered to be a small- to medium-sized tree growing from 30 to 60 feet high, its trunk reaches about 14 inches in diameter, its root system is described as “superficial” and its crown tends to be “broad” and “irregular.” Its life span ranges from 40 to 100 years while on average it lives to be up to 65 years. The brief thumbnail sketch at the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center indicates that Black Willow is the “largest and most important New World willow, with one of the most extensive ranges across the country. In the lower Mississippi Valley it attains commercial timber size, reaching 100-140 [feet] (30-42 m) in height and 4 [feet] (1.2 m) in diameter. Large trees are valuable in binding soil banks, thus preventing soil erosion and flood damage.” Its wood is considered light among the existing North American hardwoods, but even so it is reputed not to splinter easily and has been used to make “toys, crates, and barn floors.” Its ethnobotanical value has long been known wherever willows occurred around the globe and one example provided in our sources indicated that the ancient Greeks used its bark to make a tea with curative powers to treat “stiff joints and rheumatic pains.” Early modern chemists in the 1840s finally figured out the chemical properties were due to its salicylic acid, which reduced fevers and dulled or killed pain and today’s aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is the synthesized form of these naturally occurring properties. Black Willow’s extensive range in North America makes it an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

description:

Location: Unalaska Island, Eastern Aleutians, Alaska
Alt: 345m    Summer Bay Pass Comm Trail to the West
Individual Plant ID: S.rtf #1 SBP-GArg

This is the Salix rotundifolia George Argus showed me in 1995. We hiked along a WWII Comm Trail while Wilf Schofield hunted Bryophytes on the Beaver Inlet side of the pass.  At one point along the trail George stopped and asked me if I could see any willows.  I looked around and said - "No"   He then explained about Salix rotundifolia and pointed to this plant.  It has set next year's leaf buds - the small light brown globes.  Have never seen seed pods on this one, so maybe it is a male. Need to see if I can get out on that trail as the snow leaves. Think it pollinates early up there.

I've gone up to look at it every year since 1995. 

S. routidifolia are common in some spots of higher altitude wherever they can get a bit of wind cover.  Since they are SO small, they don't need much. Extraordinarily hardy!

description:
Garner State Park.  

In the vicinity of Garner State Park along the Frio River there appears to be a population of a Willow that is distinct from Salix nigra (Black Willow).  I believe it to be Salix caroliniana (Carolina Willow), the only other species of Willow that is recorded from this region of Texas.  Plants appear to be more of a large shrub/small tree than a medium-sized tree as is S. nigra, the young stems are tomentose, the undersides of the leaves are canescent, and the new growth on both leaves and stems is often reddish to a degree not seen in S. nigra in this region.  The population of S. caroliniana on the Edwards Plateau is quite disjunct from its main range in Oklahoma and eastern Kansas eastward across much of the eastern US.  S. nigra by comparison occurs extensively from west Texas to Minnesota eastward to the Atlantic coast with the only noticeable absence being peninsular Florida.

This observation is the willow tree at the heart of a feeding frenzy (?) of wasps and butterflies. 

Several species of insects are swarming specific spots on a medium sized, half-fallen but still living willow tree. I saw this same behavior at this spot last week and went back to see it in better light (not much better, it turns out). It's a tad disconcerting to stand on a rock pile slope with 1 to 2 inch wasps buzzing all around, occasionally bouncing off me or landing on me briefly, but I sucked it up and did it twice. There were at least 3 species of wasp and also individuals of at least 3 species of butterfly. I got a photo of one butterfly and three wasp species.

Salix reticulata, with rounded leaves having a shiny green reticulate-veined upper surface and small immature catkins (catkins less than the leaf length), grows and intermingles with Salix arctica, with narrow pointed leaves and large mature catkins (catkins much longer than leaf length). These species seem to behave in an ecologically neutral manner.  This site lies at the headwaters of Wyoming Creek, Line Creek Plateau, Beartooth Mountains, Park County, Wyoming.

Netleaf willow is a matted willow of subalpine to alpine habitats. The very short inconspicuous catkins are hidden among the leaves and indeed are shorter than the leaf length. The leaves are distinctive in being orbiculate (orbicular or nearly so), green and shiny above, with with the netted venation impressed on the upper surface.

Arroyo Willow (Salix lasiolepis) is a native, common shrub or tree in the Willow (Salicaceae) family that grows up to 10m (33 ft) tall in riparian habitat near rivers, streams, and springs. Peak bloom time for the yellow catkins is January-June. Indigenous people had many uses for this plant for medicines, fibers, basketry, and more. 19 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Salix+lasiolepis

Jepson eFlora https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=42855

Monterey County Wildflowers: https://montereywildflowers.com/tree-salicaceae/
Arroyo Willow (Salix lasiolepis) is a "relatively small, widely-spreading tree, perhaps the most common of the Willows. Unlike Red and Pacific Willows (Salix laevigata & lasiandra), the catkins appear before the leaves. Male flowers have only 2 stamens. The leaves are strap-shaped to elliptic to obovate, with rounded or barely pointed tips, shiny green above and bluish-white below. Although the leaves are variable, they are quite unlike the sharply pointed leaves of Red or Pacific Willows, the narrow leaves of Sandbar Willow (Salix exigua) or the broader, tomentose leaves of Sitka Willow (Salix sitchensis). The bark is smooth, very different from the furrowed bark of Red or Pacific Willows."

Flora of North America: http://floranorthamerica.org/Salix_lasiolepis
"Salix lasiolepis is polymorphic. Variety bigelovii has been recognized in coastal California and Oregon. It differs mainly in density of leaf indumentum and in having leaves tending to be slightly broader."

"This is a common willow, but easily confused with Pacific Willow (Salix lasiandra). It is one of the taller willows, with dark furrowed bark. The catkins appear at the same time as the leaves, or after them. Anthers are quite small (more like 0.5 mm than 1 mm). Male flowers have 5 stamens. Peak bloom time: December-June. Twigs are yellow-to red-brown, though in practice this is not always a reliable indicator. Leaves are 5–19 cm long, strap-shaped to lanceolate or obovate, with acuminate tips. They are green to bluish-green above, and bluish-green to whitish below. Unlike Pacific Willow, the base of the leaf blade has no glands."

Sitka Willow (Salix sitchensis) is a native, less common willow that grows along streambanks, generally near the coast. The bark is comparatively smooth. Leaves are oblanceolate to obovate, rolled under, especially basally, dull green and sparsely silky-tomentose above, densely silky or tomentose below (young leaves abaxially densely silky or woolly, adaxially sparsely-silky tomentose). Catkins appear just before or with the leaves. Male flowers have 1–2 stamens. The catkins appear longer than those of most other willows. Female catkins have distinctive silky ovaries, unlike the glabrous ovaries on the female catkins of Arroyo, Red and Pacific Willows (Salix lasiolepis, laevigata and lasiandra). Peak bloom time: March.

Narrowleaf Willow (Salix exigua), a.k.a Sandbar Willow, is a native, perennial large shrub or tree in the Willow (Salicaceae) family that grows 7 m (up to 23 ft) tall in sandy soil in many plant communties throughout California and other Western U.S. states. Jepson eFlora lists 5 subspecies. Leaves are entire (not toothed), 10 times longer than wide, and not wider than 1cm. Leaves are generally alternate, linear, and glaucous (covered with whitish or bluish waxy coating that is sometimes obscured by hairs). Petiole is 1-7 mm long. It is dioecious, with staminate and pistillate yellow catkins on separate plants, the male catkins up to 10 cm (4 inches) long, and the female catkins up to 8 cm (3 inches) long. The fruit is a cluster of capsules, each containing numerous minute seeds embedded in shiny white silk.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant as building material, basketry, tools, medicines, fuel and animal fodder. 57 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Salix+exigua

Leaf description: "abaxial surface glaucous (sometimes obscured by hairs), densely long-silky, villous or pilose to glabrescent, hairs appressed or spreading, straight or wavy, adaxial slightly glossy, sparsely or densely long-silky to glabrescent."

Willow (Salicaceae) family:
"All members of this family are dioecious, with male and female flowers borne on separate trees. All produce catkins. The male catkins appear yellow or red, depending on the color of the pollen. Female catkins appear green, until they ripen and release the fine, cottony seeds. Distinguishing the willows can be tricky: the leaf shape is generally critical. Also, whether the leaves appear before, at the same time or after the catkins is helpful. And the number of stamens in each individual flower in the male catkin is important (this can be seen with a hand lens)."

Habit: Shrub, tree; dioecious; bud scale 1, not sticky, margins generally fused (or free, overlapping). Stem: twigs generally flexible, generally not glaucous. Leaf: generally alternate; stipules generally vestigial on first leaves, leaf-like on later; mature blade linear to broadly obovate, entire to toothed, generally +- hairy; petiole glands generally 0. Inflorescence: catkin, blooming before, with, or after leaves, sessile or terminating +- short leafy or bracted shoot ("on leafy shoot" or "on bracted shoot," "catkin length" including leafless or bractless part of subtending shoot); 1 flower bract subtending each flower, deciduous or persistent, brown, black, or 2-colored (paler proximally, darker distally; darker generally +- brown). Flower: perianth reduced to adaxial nectary (rarely also with abaxial nectary, then free or fused into shallow cup). Staminate Flower: stamens (1)2(10); nectary generally 1. Narrowleaf Willow (Salix exigua), a.k.a Sandbar Willow, is a native, perennial large shrub or tree in the Willow (Salicaceae) family that grows 7 m (up to 23 ft) tall in sandy soil in many plant communties throughout California and other Western U.S. states. Jepson eFlora lists 5 subspecies. Leaves are entire (not toothed), 10 times longer than wide, and not wider than 1cm. Leaves are generally alternate, linear, and glaucous (covered with whitish or bluish waxy coating that is sometimes obscured by hairs). Petiole is 1-7 mm long. It is dioecious, with staminate and pistillate yellow catkins on separate plants, the male catkins up to 10 cm (4 inches) long, and the female catkins up to 8 cm (3 inches) long. The fruit is a cluster of capsules, each containing numerous minute seeds embedded in shiny white silk.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant as building material, basketry, tools, medicines, fuel and animal fodder. 57 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Salix+exigua

Leaf description: "abaxial surface glaucous (sometimes obscured by hairs), densely long-silky, villous or pilose to glabrescent, hairs appressed or spreading, straight or wavy, adaxial slightly glossy, sparsely or densely long-silky to glabrescent."

description: A lone male plant.

Salix caroliniana is a small shrub that can grow up to tall heights of around thirty feet and has two structures. There is a shrub, as well as a small tree, and the leaves have a spear-like form. The leaves are thin, dark green, and meet at a point, connected to a thin stem. Its common name is a Carolina Willow or Coastal Plain Willow, and from far away can seem to have a swampy appearance. A defining characteristic of a higher taxon would be Family Salicaceae. Members of this family are known to be willows, trees, or shrubs that have thin, pointed, leaf structures. Salix caroliniana was located in the wetlands. The plant was near a lake but planted on damp soil with other organisms nearby like trees and birds. For native species, Salix caroliniana can be found in Florida, North Carolina, and aligns the Atlantic Coast. The environments consist of swamps, and areas that are rich in the water supply. However, for non-native/invasive species, Salix caroliniana can be found across the North American continent, as well as stretching from parts of Canada down to Georgia. Salix caroliniana inhabits many colder areas and regions with damp soil mostly in the Northern Hemisphere. They are seen near water. Salix caroliniana also prefers to be in the sun and not receive direct shade for prolonged periods of time. This shrub interacts with the environment by absorbing moisture and nearby water. They also have the ability to cross-fertilize, meaning that male and female gametes unite by the same individual species of plant. It can be used for medicinal purposes because the bark is highly useful for those who have a fever. The scholarly article below explains the importance of the bark of willow, by utilizing modern pharmacology to help treat patients in need. The tree bark is now being used for aspirin development and exploration.

description:
This week, I began to spot fuzzy silver pussy willows along trails near the Mendenhall Glacier.  Originally, I believed that pussy willows was a common name for a particular species, but it's just the name for the fuzzy bulbs (catkins) on many willows species before they elongate and leaves appear on the branches. Pussy willows are an indicator of spring and something I look forward to seeing each year when the sun starts to shine and the snow thaws.

I struggled to find what particular willow species this is, and it will most likely be more evident in the summer with leaves.  My guess is the Sitka Willow or Salix sitchensis which has been identified near the Mendenhall glacier before. The bark and leaves of willows are food sources for Alaskan mammals such as beaver, deer and moose.  Pussy willows are a source of nectar that attract pollinators (Armstrong). 

Native people all over Alaska utilized willows traditionally for medicinal purposes for a variety of reasons such as relief from childbirth, stings, insect bites, skin trouble, headaches and cuts or scrapes (Garibaldi 47). The bark and leaves can be chewed for sores in the mouth, or poultice from leaves can be applied as a salve for skin ailments. The bark has a compound similar to aspirin that is a pain-reliever and anti-inflammatory, which explains why tooth-picks and chewing sticks were made for mouth sores.  Alaska Native people made pussy willows into a cough syrup and bathe skin infections in willow leaf tea for (Viereck).  

Armstrong, Robert H & Osborn, Marge Hermans. Life Around Mendenhall Glacier in Juneau, AK. E-book, Natural Alaska Images, 2007. https://www.naturebob.com/sites/default/files/Life%20around%20Mendenhall%20Glacier%20in%20Juneau%2C%20Alaska.pdf

Garibaldi, Ann. Medicinal Flora of the Alaska Natives. E-book, Alaska Natural Heritage Program, University of Alaska, 1999. https://accs.uaa.alaska.edu/wp-content/uploads/Medicinal_Flora_Alaska_Natives.pdf

Viereck, Eleanor G. Alaska's Wilderness Medicines. E-book, Alaska Northwest Books, 1987. http://www.ankn.uaf.edu/curriculum/Books/Viereck/viereckwillow.html

description:
Long-beaked willow growing along Spring Creek at the south end of Langhor Park, Bozeman, Montana. This willow species is fairly common along Spring Creek with the Bozeman city limits.

Long-beaked willow is a native shrub 2-4 m tall and common along streams and in wetlands from middle to high elevation throughout much of Montana, or at least the western half of the state. Its purplish twigs of the current season covered with short appressed hairs combined with leaves having whitish undersurfaces with a prominent reticulate venation are diagnostic of this willow species.

description:
These young leaves of of this willow population with strap-shaped leaves will mature to bright green, glabrous, and with margins that are often weakly serrate to dentate, which is diagnostic of dusky willow. This site lies along Spring Creek, at Langhor Park along the Gallagator Linear trail, Bozeman, Montana.

Dusky willow is a native shrub to 6 m tall. It is very similar to Salix exigua in having gray main branches and rusty red distal branches that ascend upward in broom-like fashion. Its linear leaves are bright green, glabrous, and with margins that are often weakly serrate to dentate, in contrast to those of sandbar willow, which are gray, hairy, and with entire margins. Common along rivers and streams of western Montana.

description:
Booth's willow is uncommon and sporadic in the Bozeman area. Only a few shrubs of this willow species occur along Spring Creek, including here in the Langhor Park area of the Gallagator Linear trail, Bozeman, Montana.

Booth's willow is a native shrub to 5 m tall and common along streams and lakes and generally in wetland areas from low to high elevations in western and south-central Montana. A shrub with a rounded canopy, twigs that are glabrous and yellowish, and leaves equally green on both surfaces are diagnostic of this species. Booth's willow is similar to yellow willow, Salix eriocephala (Salix lutea), except that the leaves are equally green on both surfaces in Booth's willow whereas the leaves are distinctly lighter green (glaucous) on the lower surface of the leaves of yellow willow.

description: Katahdin tablelands

This tree was about 4 feet tall, with branches about a foot long coming off of it. It was green in color with the tree trunk being a couple inches wide circumference. The leaves were about three inches long and about a half inch wide. They were jagged along the edges and came to a point at the top. This tree would be identified as an angiosperm because it bears no flowers and has "naked seeds". This tree was found in the river of Weeki  Wachee growing on the edge of the freshwater. When this organism was observed, the leaves and seeds on the plant were flourishing. It was also very warm outside the day of the observation with temperatures throughout the 90s with the sun shining. This organism's range is throughout Florida and along the Atlantic Coast up though North Carolina in edges of wetlands.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; our first visit -- but probably not our last -- because Don Fraser advised us on a "sure-thing" spot for Hayhurst's Scallopwing (we found 16+!).

We drove the entire loop (14 miles) and I separated our observations into three areas: 1; here) the loop, various generic locations; 2; the scallopwing spot) the kiosk area at the northwestern corner of the loop; and 3) the corral where they put the pregnant cows (with lots of spilled feed for icterids).

We entered the WMA at 1010 and drove the main loop counter-clockwise, arriving at the kiosk area at 1050 and remaining there until 1304), when we continued south then east along the loop (the panther encounter was at 1316). We reached the corral at 1351 and remained there until 1359. We exited the WMA at 1422. The weather at the start was sunny and 80 degrees with a light breeze; it was a few degrees warmer by the time we left.

I hesitate to mention this observation, since it is not supported by photographs, but Val and I saw what we presume was a Florida Panther (!). It appeared to have been lying in the road south of the kiosk when we spotted it at 1316. We were maybe 500 feet away when we saw an object in the road. It got up, facing us, and was an obvious feline. Val asked, "Bobcat?" but then it started moving off the road to its right (our left) and I remarked, "It has a long tail." At that point, I grabbed for my camera (sitting in my lap) -- I don't remember if I even put the car in park -- and fired off three photographs as quickly as possible, shot through the Camry's windshield. Even though such photos are typically really blurry, I had no other option. Unfortunately, the cat had slinked off the road by the time I hit the shutter (a duration of probably 5 seconds). So, no photos. I was speechless for several minutes before Val and I started discussing what we saw. It was an obvious cat bigger than a fox and maybe smaller than a Coyote, with a long tail maybe 14-16 inches long. It was pale tawny overall; we saw no radio collar

I don't know if panthers are found outside cover during the middle of the day -- especially on a day with youth hunting of Wild Turkeys occurring -- I would think not usually, but the size of the cat and its obviously long tail rule out other species other than an escaped/released cougar or other subspecies of Felis concolor. It was exciting, but since it happened so fast and especially because I got no photographs, I'm not really sure how I feel about it.

description:
There a several large native Black Willows along this small stream near the eastern edge of the Buffalo Creek watershed. These trees love water so much that if one sees them in the landscape, one can be reasonably sure of getting at least partly wet if one wants to walk around them. These are handsome and interesting trees, sometimes with unusual water roots. They can get big, but tend to have limbs close to the ground, and eventually collapse. 

My Father used to make us whistles out of sections of small Black Willow branches, by carving the mouth end and a lower notch, then tapping and rolling the piece in his hands until the outer layers separate, then pulling the woody interior out the end and planing off a an air channel on top, and a larger chamber below the notch which becomes the fipple. There are plenty of videos on how to do this on YouTube now, but Dad was really good at shaping these for a good sound. He learned this growing up on a dairy farm on a river in central Wisconsin in the 1920's and 30's.

description:
With Don Fraser, Clint Gibson, and John Reynolds; a trip mainly for John to get lots of lifers, but also another chance for me to search for Berry's Skipper and/or Brazilian Skipper, and a chance for all of us to get unexpected lifers -- we all got at least one lifer dragonfly that Don found and identified. There were lots of blooming Pickerelweeds in the ditches and marshes, so we concentrated on those areas; we searched some extensive Carolina Redroot stands but we found far fewer butterflies there. Blooming goldenrods, blazing stars, and thistles were almost non-existent. Overall, I am submitting records for 2 amphibians, 48 skippers, 12 other butterflies, 6 moths, 4 dragonflies, 2 grasshoppers, several other invertebrates, and 14 plants. I was bad about keeping notes (and there is no cell-phone coverage in the Preserve), but I think we made four or five primary stops, along Cumpressco Grade and Levee Road, before exiting at the gate at Cumpressco Grade and County Road 471. The weather at 1530 for Webster was sunny and 94 degrees ("feels like" 108) with a light breeze. I drank two gallons of Gatorade in 5 hours ... We left at 1442; I headed to Withlacoochee State Forest for my lifer Orange-fringed Orchids, while the others headed home.

I again used my Panasonic Lumix FZ80 with a non-functioning exposure dial rather than the loaner Lumix FZ200 with functioning exposure dial that Don loaned me a month or so ago. On a bright day, the lack of adjusting the exposure is not really an issue on my FZ80 -- the exposure dial broke at a very convenient setting -- plus I am much more familiar with the FZ80 compared to the FZ200, and the FZ80 has a much longer zoom (60x vs. 25x), which makes quite a difference. I soon need to decide whether to give up my FZ80 for a few weeks while I send it in for replacement, or whether I keep it and learn to live with not having a functioning exposure dial.

description:
Of the 12 species of willows likely to be found growing wild in Kentucky, Black Willow is one of the most impressive and easiest to identify. While many of our willows are large shrubs or small trees, mature Black Willows grow to be massive. Locally, the pond area at Alexandria Community Park has some of the largest Black Willows I've seen, with one approaching 2 feet in diameter and just as tall as any of the surrounding forest trees.
Black Willows also have a combination of leaf traits that make them relatively easy to tell from our other species. The leaves are alternate, and paler green below (see leaf closeups), but not white with wax or fuzz. Since many willows have white leaf undersides, this knocks out a lot of species.  The leaves are much longer (>10x) than wide and usually quite slender (less than 2 cm). The leaf bases are more rounded than tapering, and the margins are are finely serrated, with almost a tooth per millimeter. With this combination of leaf traits, even young individuals can be distinguished from our shrubby species of willows.

Narrowleaf Willow (Salix exigua), a.k.a Sandbar Willow, is a native, perennial large shrub or tree in the Willow (Salicaceae) family that grows 7 m (up to 23 ft) tall in sandy soil in many plant communties throughout California and other Western U.S. states. Jepson eFlora lists 5 subspecies. Leaves are entire (not toothed), 10 times longer than wide, and not wider than 1cm. Leaves are generally alternate, linear, and glaucous (covered with whitish or bluish waxy coating that is sometimes obscured by hairs). Petiole is 1-7 mm long. It is dioecious, with staminate and pistillate yellow catkins on separate plants, the male catkins up to 10 cm (4 inches) long, and the female catkins up to 8 cm (3 inches) long. The fruit is a cluster of capsules, each containing numerous minute seeds embedded in shiny white silk.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant as building material, basketry, tools, medicines, fuel and animal fodder. 57 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Salix+exigua

Leaf description: "abaxial surface glaucous (sometimes obscured by hairs), densely long-silky, villous or pilose to glabrescent, hairs appressed or spreading, straight or wavy, adaxial slightly glossy, sparsely or densely long-silky to glabrescent."

Scouler's Willow (Salix scouleriana) is a dioecious, native shrub or slender tree in the Willows (Salix genus) and Willow (Salicaceae) family. It grows in foothill woodlands, dry to moist forests, meadows, and in wetlands and non wetlands in many plant communities. Stems and branches are gray-brown and can be glabrous or tomentose. Young leaves are hairy. Leaves are obovate or oblanceolate to narrowly elliptic, dull green above, and short or long-silky or woolly underneath. Leaf petioles are velvety and 2--13 mm long. Peak bloom time: February-June. Indigenous people had many uses for the plant as medicine, tools, and basketry. 33 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Salix+scouleriana

Narrowleaf Willow (Salix exigua), a.k.a Sandbar Willow, is a native, perennial large shrub or tree in the Willow (Salicaceae) family that grows 7 m (up to 23 ft) tall in sandy soil in many plant communties throughout California and other Western U.S. states. Jepson eFlora lists 5 subspecies. Leaves are entire (not toothed like S. goodingii (Black Willow), 10 times longer than wide, and not wider than 1cm. Leaves are generally alternate, linear, and glaucous (covered with whitish or bluish waxy coating that is sometimes obscured by hairs). Petiole is 1-7 mm long. It is dioecious, with staminate and pistillate yellow catkins on separate plants, the male catkins up to 10 cm (4 inches) long, and the female catkins up to 8 cm (3 inches) long. The fruit is a cluster of capsules, each containing numerous minute seeds embedded in shiny white silk. 
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant as building material, basketry, tools, medicines, fuel and animal fodder. 57 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Salix+exigua

"All members of this family are dioecious, with male and female flowers borne on separate trees.  All produce catkins.  The male catkins appear yellow or red,  depending on the color of the pollen. description: This plant best matches the suggested Salix lasiolepis, commonly known as arroyo willow; a fast-growing, deciduous shrub or small tree in the willow family (Salicaceae). It is native to western North America, thriving in riparian and wetland habitats. It is a shrub or small tree. Typically growing 2–10 meters (6–33 feet) tall. Narrowleaf Willow (Salix exigua), a.k.a Sandbar Willow, is a native, perennial large shrub or tree in the Willow (Salicaceae) family that grows 7 m (up to 23 ft) tall in sandy soil in many plant communties throughout California and other Western U.S. states. Jepson eFlora lists 5 subspecies. Leaves are entire (not toothed like S. goodingii (Black Willow), 10 times longer than wide, and not wider than 1cm. Leaves are generally alternate, linear, and glaucous (covered with whitish or bluish waxy coating that is sometimes obscured by hairs). Petiole is 1-7 mm long. It is dioecious, with staminate and pistillate yellow catkins on separate plants, the male catkins up to 10 cm (4 inches) long, and the female catkins up to 8 cm (3 inches) long. The fruit is a cluster of capsules, each containing numerous minute seeds embedded in shiny white silk.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant as building material, basketry, tools, medicines, fuel and animal fodder. 57 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Salix+exigua

"All members of this family are dioecious, with male and female flowers borne on separate trees. All produce catkins. The male catkins appear yellow or red, depending on the color of the pollen. Female catkins appear green, until they ripen and release the fine, cottony seeds. Distinguishing the willows can be tricky: the leaf shape is generally critical. Also, whether the leaves appear before, at the same time or after the catkins is helpful. And the number of stamens in each individual flower in the male catkin is important (this can be seen with a hand lens)."
